sections.report:
**Walk (working notes).** Bash was refused, so I couldn't run the crop script. The image is about 1280×800, roughly one screen, so I worked from the whole image.

First read: the eye lands on the bold sans headline "Notes for ferry passengers" at the top left, then drops into four even serif paragraphs. It reads as a plain information page for people who use a river ferry. It feels calm, quiet and sparse, and the right ~40% of the frame is empty. Assumed job: give passengers the practical facts they need to use the ferry.

- Can a first-time viewer say in one sentence what this is for? yes
- Do image and headline make one idea? yes (there's no main image; the headline and the text agree)
- Does every element do a job? yes (no rules, boxes or ornament)
- Do type, colour and shape share one mood? yes (bold grotesque headline over a book serif is a standard pairing, all one dark neutral)
- Is the copy finished, with no placeholder text or typos? yes
- Does each kind of element look the same everywhere? yes (all four paragraphs share one style and spacing)
- Do colour, shape and direction carry the right mood? yes (calm and neutral suits notices)
- Does each heading name what its section holds? yes

Every line is yes, so step 5 has no entries to open.

---

**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
None.

One copy point has no checklist line, but the director should weigh it. The facts a passenger will plan around are vague or contradict each other, and none of them can be checked:
- Paragraph 1 (y≈147–233) says "every forty minutes between early morning and late evening" with no times.
- Paragraph 3 (y≈415–472) says "the last crossing leaves the quay before dusk" and "one boat each hour" in winter.
- Paragraph 1 doesn't say it's the summer timetable, so a reader in winter could read "every forty minutes" as true now.
- "Before dusk" moves by an hour or more across the season.
- The only fix it offers is the printed timetables at the landings, which you can only read once you're already there.
- "Last spring" (paragraph 4, y≈521) goes out of date without anyone noticing.

The result: passengers can't plan a trip from this page and may miss the last boat. The fix is to give real first and last departure times for each season, say which season each frequency belongs to, and point to where the current timetable is online. This is a defect on common sense; no catalog entry covers it. Weight: major. Times are what passengers act on and later hold the operator to.

**What's working.**
- The page is reduced to the text alone. There's no ornament, box or rule, so nothing competes with the words, and that suits a notice people read once and act on.
- The two typefaces read as one voice. The heavy sans headline and the warm serif body share one dark neutral colour and an even rhythm, so the piece feels calm and trustworthy, not assembled from parts.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 8 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

sections.report:
Walk (working notes): The eye lands on the title "Notes for ferry passengers" (about x120–594, y65–105), then moves down into the four paragraphs of body text. It reads as an information page for ferry riders. I couldn't run the crop script because Bash was denied, but the image is about 1280×800, roughly one screen, so I worked from the whole image.
- Does one element stand clearly above the rest? Yes. The title is a bold sans at about twice the body size and sits alone at the top.
- Can you tell each text level from the next at a glance? Yes. There are only two levels, title and body, and the step between them is large.
- Do headings that are larger than the text also differ in another way? Yes. The title is a heavy sans, the body a regular serif, and the title also looks a little darker.

Every line was yes, so there were no entries to open in step 5.

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
1. **The title clearly leads.** "Notes for ferry passengers" (about x120–594, y65–105) is a heavy sans at about twice the body size, with clear space below it. The eye knows where to start, and the page has no competing element.
2. **The title differs from the body in more than size.** It changes size, weight and form together: a bold sans against a regular serif. So the two levels can't be confused, even at a glance or when the page is shrunk. Keep this pairing if subheadings are added.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

sections.report:
I checked one section, arrangement and space. It applies to this image, and I found one minor problem. The image is 1280 × 800 px, small enough to judge whole, so no crops were made. I assumed the piece is a desktop web page for ferry passengers, since I was told nothing about it.

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does the visual weight balance, with no side, crowded or empty, that makes the page look about to tip?** No.
   - **Where:** All the dark weight sits in a column from x≈120 to x≈775 and y≈65 to y≈560: the bold heading plus four dense serif paragraphs. The right side, from x≈775 to 1280 (about 40% of the width), is empty from top to bottom, and nothing there offsets the column.
   - **What the viewer experiences:** The page leans left and looks unfinished. It reads less like a chosen asymmetric layout and more like a sidebar or picture failed to load. The text itself still reads fine.
   - **Why:** Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, chapter "Balance": a heavy side needs a counterweight, and a lopsided composition with no visible intent is a fault.
   - **Fix direction:** Either move the column toward the centre so the left margin takes a bigger share of the free space, or give the right side something small but strong to weigh against the column. A box with the next sailing times or the winter timetable would fit, since that is the content passengers act on. If this column sits on a site grid whose right column is just empty on this page, the problem is in the template, not in this page.
   - **Kind and weight:** Taste, minor.

**What's working.**
- **Spacing shows the groups.** Lines within a paragraph are about 28 px apart, gaps between paragraphs are about 48 px, and the heading sits about 40 px above the body. So each paragraph reads as one unit and the heading clearly belongs to the text below it.
- **One shared left edge.** The heading and all four paragraphs line up exactly on x≈120 with no near-misses, so the column reads as a single firm block and the eye runs straight down it.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** I can't tell whether the column re-centres or the right side fills at other viewport widths. That decides whether the empty right side is a real defect or only a quirk of this capture width, so it's worth checking in a live browser.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 12 yes, 1 no (visual weight balances).

**Section.** Text: applies. The image is a single page of headed prose, about 1280×800. My Bash calls were refused, so I couldn't run `crop.mjs` or `entries.mjs`. I judged from the whole image, which is about one screen and would have produced no crops anyway.

**Findings**
1. **Do paragraphs and columns break cleanly, with no lone short word on a last line and no heading at the foot of a column?** The second paragraph ("Bicycles ride on the lower deck…") ends with the single word "crossing." on its own line, at about x 120–200, y 367. A three-line paragraph with a one-word fourth line ends on a stub. The extra line also makes that paragraph look longer and looser than the others. In a short page of four blocks, the stub is the one break in the otherwise even texture. Bringhurst treats this kind of runt as something to fix when setting text. To fix it, rewrite a few words or pull the line back slightly so at least two words, ideally a short phrase, land on the last line. On the web, `text-wrap: pretty` or a non-breaking space before the last word does this. Convention. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- The body size and line length suit a page someone reads closely. The serif body looks about 19 px. The longest lines run about 70–72 characters ("takes about twelve minutes in calm weather, and a little longer when the"), which is inside 45–75. Leading looks about 1.5, open enough for that length without the lines drifting apart. The column reads comfortably and stays put.
- The two typefaces clearly contrast and don't clash. A bold grotesque sans for the heading sits against a reading serif for the body, with nothing that nearly matches. Paragraphs are marked by space alone with no indent, and the first one after the heading is flush. These choices give the page a clean, single plan to keep.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 29 yes, 1 no (paragraphs break cleanly, no lone short word on a last line), 0 unsure

sections.report:
Walk (Color): 1. Small palette: yes. 2. Strong colour kept small: yes. 3. Clear light/dark range: yes. 4. Warm/cool placement: yes. 5. Matching colours look the same: yes. 6. No vibrating edges: yes. 7. Status colours used only for their meaning: yes. 8. Meaning not shown by colour alone: yes. 9. Dark theme background: yes. No line was `no` or `unsure`, so there were no entries to open for step 5. The image is about one screen (1280×800), so I judged it from the whole image without crops.

**Section.** Color: applies. It's a plain text page with near-black type on a white background and no hue anywhere.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **Contrast.** The heading (about x 120–595, y 65–105) and all four body paragraphs (x 120–775, y 135–560) are dark charcoal on white. That's the strongest light-to-dark range there is, so the text reads easily and the page's structure survives in grayscale. For a passenger notice that people read quickly, often on a phone outside, this is right.
- **A single neutral range.** The piece uses one gray family and no accent colour. The heading stands out through size and weight, not colour, so nothing competes for attention and no colour carries meaning that a colour-blind reader would miss. The heading also looks a touch darker or cooler than the body text. If that's on purpose it's harmless; if not, it's too small to matter.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure
